title_original: The Poetry Caravan: From Dakar to Venice, Koyo Kouoh’s Vision in Motion

blocks.text: Revived at the 61st Venice Biennale, Koyo Kouoh’s Poetry Caravan became a central expression of her vision: a moving celebration of language, memory and artistic exchange. Bringing together poets, artists and musicians, it traced a journey that began in West Africa more than a quarter-century earlier.
Suzette Bell-Roberts

The sound of a West African kora drifted through the Giardini, accompanied by saxophone improvisations and the voices of poets moving between the national pavilions. The gathering followed no conventional exhibition route. Instead, performances unfolded at successive stops, drawing visitors into a procession where poetry, music, and movement became inseparable. First conceived by Koyo Kouoh in 1999 as a journey from Dakar to Timbuktu with nine African poets, the Poetry Caravan was revived in Venice a year after her death, carrying the spirit of that original undertaking into the heart of the Biennale, where spoken word and shared listening offered a different way of encountering art. Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.caption: Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.text: The original journey grew out of Kouoh’s interest in artistic and intellectual exchange beyond conventional cultural institutions. Travelling across West Africa, the poets recited, chanted, and shared their work, letting the changing landscape and encounters along the route become part of the creative process. The road provided the conditions through which poetry could circulate, gathering new meanings through conversation and performance. Rather than presenting literature as a finished work awaiting an audience, the caravan understood artistic expression as something continually shaped by its surroundings.

Its destination, Timbuktu, carried particular historical significance. For centuries, the city had been a centre of scholarship, manuscript production and intellectual exchange, connected through trans-Saharan networks to communities across North and West Africa. The journey evoked these histories alongside the traditions of the griot, whose storytelling, music and recitation have preserved collective memory across generations. By bringing contemporary poets into dialogue with these traditions, Kouoh drew attention to the different ways knowledge is created and transmitted, recognising African oral cultures as established systems of thought with their own authority.

The journey also suggested a different relationship between artistic production and geography. Its significance did not depend solely upon the historical importance of Timbuktu or the cultural associations of Dakar, but upon the distances travelled between them. Each encounter introduced the possibility of a new audience, a different language or an unexpected exchange. The poets participated in a developing experience rather than performing a predetermined programme. In this sense, the caravan was both a literary undertaking and an experiment in how artistic communities might be formed through movement.

This understanding became central to Kouoh’s curatorial practice. Throughout her career, she questioned the structures through which contemporary art is presented, interpreted and valued, advocating for institutions that encourage intellectual exchange and sustained relationships rather than merely accumulating exhibitions. The Poetry Caravan anticipated this approach by making collaboration and participation integral to the work itself. Its significance resided as much in the relationships established during the journey as in the individual poems performed along the way.

The project’s return took shape within In Minor Keys , the exhibition Kouoh conceived for the 61st Venice Biennale before her death in May 2025. Having established its intellectual framework and curatorial direction, she left a vision her team carried forward. Her approach proposed a different register of engagement within an international exhibition frequently associated with scale, visibility and spectacle. Attentiveness, hospitality, intimacy and meaningful encounters were central to her thinking, and the revival of the Poetry Caravan brought these ideas into the physical experience of moving through the Giardini. Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.caption: Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.text: On 7 May 2026, during the Biennale’s opening preview, the procession unfolded across seven stations before the exhibition opened to the public on 9 May. Bringing together poets, writers, visual artists, and musicians from Africa, the Caribbean, the Americas, the Middle East, Europe, and South Asia, the gathering moved between recitation, chanting, song, and improvisation. María Magdalena Campos-Pons addressed Kouoh in an invocation, establishing an atmosphere in which remembrance and artistic expression became closely intertwined. The performance was both a tribute to the curator and a continuation of a project whose meaning had always depended on its participants’ contributions.

The diversity of those participants was fundamental to the experience. Senegalese novelist Ken Bugul and Cameroon-born writer and theatre-maker Werewere Liking connected the gathering to African literary and oral traditions. At the same time, Natalie Diaz, Robin Coste Lewis and Batool Abu Akleen brought perspectives shaped by Indigenous histories, the politics of representation and the experience of war. Their practices demonstrate how poetry can challenge dominant historical narratives, preserve experiences excluded from official records and give form to realities that resist straightforward representation.

Momtaza Mehri, Christian Campbell, Rodney Saint-Éloi, Mohsen Emadi and Manee Mohale extended these conversations across experiences of migration, colonialism and belonging. Rather than constructing a singular narrative around cultural identity or displacement, the procession allowed distinct histories and literary approaches to coexist. Anne Waldman’s experimental approach to performance introduced another dimension, emphasising the relationship between language, breath, and rhythm, and the human voice’s capacity to communicate beyond the written page.

The gathering’s international character mattered precisely because it did not try to erase differences among its participants. Their practices emerged from distinct political circumstances, literary histories, and cultural traditions, yet the procession created a setting where these experiences could be encountered together. Connections developed through the succession of performances and the audience’s experience of moving between them, without requiring every contribution to illustrate a single curatorial argument.

Visual artists complicated these boundaries further. Gabrielle Goliath’s engagement with sound, testimony and collective mourning brought particular resonance to an event shaped by Kouoh’s absence. At the same time, Rajashri Goody and Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung contributed perspectives on how knowledge is produced, circulated, and valued. Their participation expanded the gathering beyond literary performance, recognising listening, remembrance and collective engagement as artistic practices in their own right. Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.caption: Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.text: Music was equally important to the caravan’s character. Senegalese kora musician, established a sonic connection to West African traditions of storytelling and historical transmission. At the same time, saxophonist Philippe Mall, Kouoh’s husband, contributed an intimate tribute through his composition Wise One , dedicated to her, and an interpretation of Nature Boy . Lebanese musician and visual artist Raed Yassin introduced an experimental approach to improvisation, alongside Kamaal Malak’s interdisciplinary contribution. The interaction between instruments and voices created a shifting soundscape in which music was not simply an accompaniment to poetry but an independent form of expression.

The relationship between the kora and saxophone was particularly evocative. Their contrasting musical histories and tonal qualities brought different traditions into proximity without requiring them to merge into a single idiom. The kora’s ties to West African oral history recalled the caravan’s origins, while the saxophone introduced a language of improvisation that could respond to the procession’s changing atmosphere. Together with the spoken word, the instruments established a dialogue in which rhythm, melody and silence became integral to the experience.

The movement between stations was equally important. The changing acoustics of the Giardini, the presence of visitors and the intervals between contributions shaped the performance, allowing moments of silence to carry their own significance. Poetry and music occupied the same public spaces as the national pavilions, temporarily altering how audiences navigated the Venice Biennale. The procession invited visitors to encounter art through duration and participation rather than through the rapid accumulation of visual impressions.

Within an exhibition of the Biennale’s scale, this interruption mattered. The density of installations, the distance between venues, and the pressure of limited viewing time can push visitors to move quickly between works, often privileging those that make the strongest immediate visual impression. The Poetry Caravan operated according to a different logic. Its meaning developed gradually and could not be reduced to a single image or moment. Experiencing it required a willingness to follow, listen, and remain attentive to the changing relationships between performers and their surroundings. Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.caption: Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.text: The experience also unsettled the conventional distinction between performer and audience. Visitors were not merely observing an event from a fixed position; their movement became part of its unfolding. As the procession advanced, the gathering continually changed in composition and scale, creating temporary relationships among people who might otherwise have encountered one another only in passing. This participation did not eliminate the distinction between artist and spectator, but it made the audience’s presence more consequential to the work’s character.

Yet the caravan did not entirely escape the spectacle it appeared to challenge. Its visibility and the prominence of its participants inevitably attracted attention, particularly within the charged atmosphere of the Biennale’s opening days. What distinguished it was how that attention was distributed. Rather than concentrating the audience’s gaze on a monumental installation or a single artistic personality, the caravan let different voices and instruments emerge in succession. The experience was collective without being anonymous, recognising individual contributions while refusing to establish a hierarchy among them.

The journey from West Africa to Venice also exposed an important tension between cultural traditions and institutional authority. Kouoh’s original project had developed outside the established structures of the international art world, drawing upon intellectual histories that did not require validation through European institutions. Its revival in the Giardini did not confer legitimacy upon these traditions; they already possessed their own histories, methods and forms of cultural authority. Instead, their presence challenged the Biennale to accommodate artistic practices that exceed the conventions of the exhibition format.

This distinction was central to the broader ambition of In Minor Keys . Kouoh was not simply proposing a quieter exhibition within an otherwise unchanged institutional framework. Her vision questioned the values that determine what receives attention, whose knowledge shapes artistic discourse and how audiences might engage with work beyond the demands of spectacle. The Poetry Caravan translated these concerns into an experience in which oral expression, movement and participation became the means through which artistic ideas circulated. Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.caption: Image courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

blocks.text: Its commemorative significance was equally complex. Kouoh’s absence inevitably shaped the gathering, but the procession resisted reducing her contribution to a fixed account of achievements. Instead, the artists continued a project that had always depended upon the exchange of ideas and the formation of relationships. The gathering allowed grief, gratitude and celebration to coexist without resolving them into a singular statement of remembrance. In doing so, it showed how a curatorial vision can remain active through others’ practices, acquiring new meanings as circumstances change.

The distance between Dakar and Timbuktu and the pathways of the Giardini could scarcely be more different. Yet the relationship between the two journeys was more consequential than their shared form. Both recognised that artistic expression is shaped by the conditions in which it takes place, and that knowledge circulates through encounters as well as through objects and institutions. In Venice, these ideas acquired renewed urgency within an exhibition whose international prominence can sometimes overshadow the more intimate exchanges through which art transforms perception.

The procession left no permanent monument. Its significance resided in the temporary reorganisation of the Biennale’s public spaces, where the authority of the displayed object gave way to the presence of the speaking and listening body. What began as a journey across West Africa had become a proposition about the international exhibition itself: that its value need not be determined solely by the artworks it contains, but also by the knowledge it allows to circulate and the relationships it makes possible. In bringing the Poetry Caravan to Venice, Kouoh’s curatorial vision found expression not through another object to be viewed, but through an experience that asked audiences to reconsider what it means to encounter art.
